title: Slow-Roast Pork Shoulder
subtitle: Eight-hour roast pork with crisp crackling
excerpt: Pork shoulder roasted very slowly for 8 hours until the meat falls apart, with a final blast of high heat to crisp the rind into crackling. Serve with apple sauce and roast potatoes.

recipe.sourceNotes: Slow-roasting a whole pork shoulder bone-in at low temperature is one of the most reliable methods for producing fall-apart pork. The long cooking at 150 C breaks down the collagen in the shoulder into gelatin, which makes the meat moist and tender. The rind, if dry and well-scored, will blister and crackle during the initial high-heat blast or the final high-heat finish. Pork shoulder (or blade) is significantly cheaper than leg and better suited to long slow roasting: it has more fat and connective tissue that melt during the long cook.

recipeTools.notes: A large, heavy roasting tin with at least 5 cm sides to catch the drippings.

content.text: The rind must be completely dry before it goes into the oven: moisture prevents crackling from forming. Pat dry with kitchen paper and leave the pork uncovered in the fridge overnight if possible. Score the rind in close parallel lines with a sharp knife. Rub salt into the scored lines: the salt draws out more moisture and seasons the crackling. The long slow roast requires no attention: just put it in and leave it.

items.preparation: bone-in, rind on, rind scored deeply at 1 cm intervals

content.text: The night before: pat the pork completely dry. Score the rind. Rub 2 teaspoons of salt into the scored rind and the flesh. Leave uncovered in the fridge overnight to dry out.

On the day: remove the pork from the fridge 1 hour before cooking. Heat the oven to 220 C / fan 200 C / gas 7. Make small cuts in the flesh and press half a garlic clove and a small sprig of rosemary into each. Mix the fennel seeds, remaining salt, pepper, and olive oil into a paste and rub over the flesh (not the rind). Place rind-side up in the roasting tin. Pour the wine into the bottom of the tin.

Roast at 220 C for 30 minutes until the rind starts to blister. Reduce the heat to 150 C / fan 130 C / gas 2. Roast for a further 7 to 7.5 hours until the meat pulls apart easily with two forks. The pan juices will have reduced to a sticky glaze; add a splash of water if the tin looks dry.

If the crackling is not fully crisped, increase the oven to 240 C and cook for a further 10 to 15 minutes, watching carefully. Rest for 20 minutes before pulling the meat apart. Serve with apple sauce, roast potatoes, and the pan drippings thinned with a little stock.
